read.passage: When Abdullah joined his school's discussion club, he thought the goal was to win every argument. In his first meeting, he talked over everyone and called other people's ideas 'useless'. Afterwards, the club leader, an older student, took him aside. 'What makes a good speaker,' he said, 'isn't how loudly you talk. It's how well you listen.' Over the next few weeks, Abdullah practised softening his opinions with phrases like 'I'm not entirely sure that …' and inviting quieter members to speak. He also learnt to judge ideas fairly by looking at their strengths before their drawbacks. By the end of the term, the members had chosen him as their new chairperson, something he would never have imagined on his first day.

qs.q: What did Abdullah do in his first meeting?
options: He invited quiet members to speak.
qs.cando: Can understand articles on social and scientific topics.

read2.passage: Headlines regularly warn that teenagers spend too long on screens, yet researchers increasingly argue that the question is not how much time young people spend online, but what they do there. A recent study of two thousand students found that those who used screens mainly for creative activities, such as editing videos or coding, reported higher well-being than those who mostly scrolled through social media. What worried researchers most was not screen use itself, but its tendency to replace sleep and exercise. The authors therefore recommend that families focus less on strict time limits and more on keeping phones out of bedrooms at night. Not everyone is convinced: some doctors point out that the study relied on students' own reports, which may not be accurate.

qs.q: According to the researchers, what matters most?
options: how many hours they spend online
